concepts.decision: Use to prevent one process from reading or changing another’s memory.
concepts.definition: Hardware and OS enforcement that separates address spaces by privilege or process.
concepts.failureExample: A memory-corruption flaw gains access to a more-privileged address region.
concepts.label: Memory Protection

concepts.decision: Use when independent workloads or privilege levels must not affect each other.
concepts.definition: Separation that confines a process’s resources and privileges from other processes.
concepts.failureExample: A plugin can alter the host application’s files and tokens.
concepts.label: Process Isolation

concepts.decision: Use when key protection and measured boot evidence are required.
concepts.definition: Hardware component that can protect keys and measurements for platform trust decisions.
concepts.failureExample: A device starts altered firmware but reports a normal state without attestation.
concepts.label: Trusted Platform Module

concepts.decision: Use when preventing unauthorized firmware or bootloader changes matters.
concepts.definition: Startup verification that permits approved boot components under a trust policy.
concepts.failureExample: A modified bootloader loads before endpoint protections start.
concepts.label: Secure Boot

concepts.decision: Choose for a defined data state, threat, key custody, and endpoint assumption.
concepts.definition: Cryptographic protection of selected information states using managed keys.
concepts.failureExample: A stolen storage device exposes unencrypted records.
concepts.label: Encryption

concepts.decision: Assess custody, separation, recovery, rotation, and access to every key.
concepts.definition: Lifecycle control for generating, storing, using, rotating, recovering, and destroying keys.
concepts.failureExample: A backup contains encrypted data and its recovery key in the same exposed location.
concepts.label: Key Management

concepts.decision: Use when workload separation benefits exceed hypervisor and management dependencies.
concepts.definition: Use of a hypervisor to multiplex isolated workloads on shared hardware.
concepts.failureExample: One overprivileged console changes multiple guest networks and snapshots.
concepts.label: Virtualization

concepts.decision: Protect, retain, correlate, and review logs according to the use case.
concepts.definition: Recorded security-relevant events used for accountability, detection, and investigation.
concepts.failureExample: An attacker deletes local logs before the incident is noticed.
concepts.label: Logging

concepts.decision: Use where software-only trust cannot adequately establish the initial state.
concepts.definition: Trusted hardware basis for verifying platform identity, measurements, or key protection.
concepts.failureExample: A remote attestation relies on measurements an attacker can rewrite in software.
concepts.label: Hardware Root Of Trust

concepts.decision: Require unique identities, strong authentication, scope, review, and emergency handling.
concepts.definition: Control of high-authority accounts through attributable, limited, protected administration.
concepts.failureExample: A shared root account makes a destructive configuration change untraceable.
concepts.label: Privileged Account Management

misconceptions.claim: A TPM makes a whole system trustworthy.
misconceptions.correction: It can anchor specific measurements or keys; trust still depends on configuration, software, administration, and response processes.

outcome: Match a platform capability to a protection objective and identify the assumption that must also hold.

sections.body: Memory and process isolation limit one workload’s ability to read or alter another. A hardware root of trust and secure boot can provide evidence about approved startup state. Encryption protects information in selected states but depends on key management and endpoint handling. Virtualization can isolate workloads but introduces management-plane and hypervisor dependencies. Logging supports detection and accountability when protected and reviewed.
keyPoints: Match the capability to the asset, state, and threat.
Management planes and key paths are part of the architecture.
sections.title: Capabilities protect different layers

sections.body: A TPM cannot compensate for an untrusted administrator or poor recovery process. Encryption cannot protect data after an authorized endpoint displays it. Isolation can fail through configuration, shared services, vulnerable management interfaces, or side channels. Define attestation, patching, privileged administration, monitoring, backup, and incident response alongside the capability.
keyPoints: Claims must include scope and residual risk.
Operational controls preserve the capability’s intended protection.
sections.title: Design for limits and operation

sections.body: Memory protection separates process or privilege address spaces; a TPM or other hardware root can protect keys and measurements; encryption and decryption protect selected data states under managed keys; secure boot and attestation can provide startup or configuration evidence; isolation and virtualization separate workloads while adding hypervisor and management-plane dependencies; and logging supports accountability when protected and reviewed. Select a capability by asset, state, threat, privilege boundary, integration path, administrator, update mechanism, and evidence. A capability is not a guarantee: a compromised privileged manager, exported key, weak recovery path, disabled measurement, shared service, or unreviewed configuration can defeat the intended claim. Layer operations, monitoring, access control, and recovery around the platform feature.
keyPoints: State the protected property, boundary, decision owner, operating evidence, and residual failure mode.
Treat architecture controls as lifecycle commitments: configuration, monitoring, response, maintenance, and recovery determine whether the claim holds.
sections.title: Bound capability claims with configuration and operational assumptions
